AI has entered the portals of educational institutions - schools, colleges, universities - at a speed
that makes the entry of computers a generation ago seem glacial. Hrrmphs regarding the danger it
poses as a detour for critical thinking in young minds is less Luddite than those who believed
computers would signal the end of civilisation as we knew it. So, without sounding alarmist,
guidance and policy must keep pace with rapid proliferation of generative AI in education. The
urgency is driven by the fact that tech companies are turning to schools and universities across the
world as potential consumers and clients - apart from the free options already available. In this
case, 'caveat emptor' goes beyond the usual warning.


The aggressive marketing draws on the old playbook of computers to improve computer literacy.
Again, Fomo is driving schools to sign up. For the education system at large, there is no need to
shun this technology. On the contrary, familiarity is necessary to ensure that a new generation
learns new ways of using it. Which is why it's more than helpful to draw on learnings from the old
computer access programmes to develop necessary guidance for teachers, education
administrators, curriculum developers and parents. Training on how to use AI in classrooms and
beyond, as well as a tool to enhance teaching and the learning experience without undermining
efforts to enhance critical thinking, cognitive skills and learning outcomes is essential.

learning loss. Efforts must be made to disincentivise AI as the option for students to 'outsource'
their learning and learning outcomes. Make it an integral tool, not cheat sheet.

From childhood, I carry a memory both tender and vivid of the gentle clip-clop of tongas outside
railway stations, their worn wooden wheels turning patiently, drawn by horses whose names we
never knew. We would climb aboard as a family, and those slow rides offered a sense of rhythm,
simplicity, and wonder. Recently, that memory came rushing back to me as I saw a photograph
from Gaza. A donkey-drawn cart creaked forward under the weight of a fleeing family: Three
children clinging to their parents, bags of belongings teetering in the back, and the donkey pulling
on, battered and thin.


That image broke me. Not just for what it shows of human suffering, but for the silent resilience
of the donkey, an animal often mocked and neglected, yet carrying the unbearable burdens of war
and its aftermath. The donkey does not speak, does not choose, does not understand the
abstractions in whose name wars are waged. Yet in its mute endurance, it exposes the obscenity


Head Office: Plot No.6, Ground Floor, Opp. Mio Coworks, Saket, Saidulajab, New Delhi – 110030   12minutestoclat.com


of a politics that blesses destruction while speaking the language of security and destiny.
Anonymous and indispensable, the donkey becomes the last symbol of unconditional care and the
innocent voiceless victims in a place where modern systems have collapsed, a silent labourer of
war for whom there is no manger waiting at the end.


In Gaza, the donkey indeed emerges as a silent comrade in the struggle for survival. What
devastates me most is the helplessness of it all. The image of children sitting in the cart, innocent
and wide-eyed, on their way to nowhere. The father walking alongside, powerless to protect them.
The donkey limping on, trying to do what it was never asked to do. And yet, the cart still carries a
strange cosiness. The children huddle together, as if pretending this were just a journey to a picnic,
not exile. The donkey walks, tired but unyielding, as if it, too, is hoping for a warm stable to
welcome him on the other side of misery. In this cold, calculated, and unfeeling world, it is the
cart in Gaza that underscores what dignity looks like in ruins, in movement, in endurance.


Though a relic in a world that worships acceleration, the cart resists the tyranny of haste, moving
not with urgency, but symbolically suggesting the “politics of slowness”. I see a quiet, almost
unbearable dignity in the image of the donkey. In a time when human conscience lies buried
beneath propaganda and spectacle, it is this humble companion that bears the weight of their
survival and the cold, calculated silence of a world that refuses to care.

donkey-in-gaza-broke-me-10460924/

It’s 15 years since venture capitalist Marc Andreessen said, “software is eating the world”, and he
couldn’t have been more right. We have an app for everything now – multiple apps actually. So,
in a nod to Darwin, software has been eating software. Take for example the news that Google’s
Gemini AI models will power Apple’s Siri virtual assistant. This marks the end of a race that
started in 2010 when Google’s Android OS, and Apple, acquired voice command capabilities
almost simultaneously. Amazon’s Alexa and Microsoft’s Cortana were also hot contenders at one
point. But a Gemini-powered Siri in 2026 proves that software matters more than hardware.


Thanks to the Apple deal, Google’s parent Alphabet has cracked the $4tn valuation club, populated
by just one other entity currently – Nvidia. Of course, markets are fickle. Microsoft and Apple
were there, slipped out, and may be back anytime. What matters is value measured in terms of life-
changing impact. And there’s no doubt the world is much more livable thanks to software.
Everything from food to rides and flights is a click away. We can connect with friends on foreign
shores for free. We can have our fill of movies and songs for small monthly fees. Software makes
it possible for anyone, anywhere to get the best education. It’s improved healthcare. Farmers get
better weather forecasts and market news. Factories are safer, and product quality better, again
thanks to software. Even war is now software’s playfield. Israel’s Lavender targeting system can
identify Hamas operatives; Ukraine’s Op Spider Web was a modern take on the Trojan horse.


Hardware still matters – ask Boeing. But software is the key differentiator, the game changer.
German carmakers have struggled against the Chinese not because their motors and chassis are
inferior, but because the Chinese make slicker OS and interfaces for EVs, thanks to their extensive

questions.stimulus:
It’s 15 years since venture capitalist Marc Andreessen said, “software is eating the world”, and he
couldn’t have been more right. We have an app for everything now – multiple apps actually. So,
in a nod to Darwin, software has been eating software. Take for example the news that Google’s
Gemini AI models will power Apple’s Siri virtual assistant. This marks the end of a race that
started in 2010 when Google’s Android OS, and Apple, acquired voice command capabilities
almost simultaneously. Amazon’s Alexa and Microsoft’s Cortana were also hot contenders at one
point. But a Gemini-powered Siri in 2026 proves that software matters more than hardware.


Thanks to the Apple deal, Google’s parent Alphabet has cracked the $4tn valuation club, populated
by just one other entity currently – Nvidia. Of course, markets are fickle. Microsoft and Apple
were there, slipped out, and may be back anytime. What matters is value measured in terms of life-
changing impact. And there’s no doubt the world is much more livable thanks to software.
Everything from food to rides and flights is a click away. We can connect with friends on foreign
shores for free. We can have our fill of movies and songs for small monthly fees. Software makes
it possible for anyone, anywhere to get the best education. It’s improved healthcare. Farmers get
better weather forecasts and market news. Factories are safer, and product quality better, again
thanks to software. Even war is now software’s playfield. Israel’s Lavender targeting system can
identify Hamas operatives; Ukraine’s Op Spider Web was a modern take on the Trojan horse.


Hardware still matters – ask Boeing. But software is the key differentiator, the game changer.
German carmakers have struggled against the Chinese not because their motors and chassis are
inferior, but because the Chinese make slicker OS and interfaces for EVs, thanks to their extensive
experience of making smartphones. With its vast pool of tech talent, India can also be a software
powerhouse. After all, Alphabet and Microsoft have been helmed by Indian-origin engineers for
years. To make software, we don’t need lithium and cobalt mines. We already write a lot of code

for MNCs at our GCCs, and that’s great, but what we need are brands of our own. Our own world-
beating products powered by our own software.

Is Greenland next? That’s the big geopolitical question, fanned daily by Trump & Co. He pulled
out the national security imperative on Sunday. On Monday, his homeland security adviser
Stephen Miller said, “Nobody’s going to fight the US militarily over the future of Greenland.” Fair
point. Denmark, which has controlled Greenland for 300 years, isn’t quite the military power it
was when it harassed the Mughals in Bay of Bengal for 50 years in the 17th century. But just
because Danes have only 16,000 soldiers now doesn’t mean Trump should grab Greenland. Yes,
its strategic location, access to Arctic Ocean, rare earths, and probably billions of barrels of oil,
make it irresistible for him. But this is Europe. There’s no fig leaf of drugs and “invasion” by
immigrants this time.


So, a grab – Danes themselves say it would take five choppers at most – would look awfully bad
on Trump’s dossier. Even if he doesn’t care about Nato. Instead, as Trump said last year, “I think
we’re going to get it, one way or the other,” he should try the “other” tack. His old pitch about
investing “billions of dollars” to create new jobs, to make Greenlanders rich, is a good idea. But
since they are almost as rich as Americans in PPP dollar terms, he must sweeten the deal.
Considering that 85% of them earlier opposed absorption by US, Trump should offer all 58,000 of

them $1mn per head, plus US citizenship as icing on the cake, payable after they consent in a
referendum. It will cost US just $58bn – a mere 0.15% of $38tn US national debt. Btw, Trump’s
new ballroom, and retrofitting his Qatari Boeing, are likely to cost over $1bn.


This isn’t an outrageous proposal. People change nationality for economic advantage all the time.
Remember, 56% of Greenlanders are keen on independence from Denmark. And Denmark, which
sold its Caribbean colonies to US in 1917, may be less reluctant than it seems. If this offer
persuades Greenlanders, Trump gets Greenland, and there’s no stain of invasion. Let the dollar
talk.

Three out of four spices known to humans are grown in India, which produces nearly half the
global spice output. Three-quarters of that ends up in Indian curries. The leftovers are exported to
200 countries as inexpensive raw spices. Bulk of our exports are confined to a handful of spices
and head to a few countries. China is one, where Indian spices are blended, and essential
components extracted for food and medicinal use. This is where the money is in the spice business.
And India is not doing enough about it.


For a start, production must rise faster, so that more spices can be exported. This would involve
productivity improvements since area under spice cultivation is limited. Agricultural research has
a big role to play. But central and state governments have been tight-fisted about funding it. Yield
improvement through pesticide use runs up against phytosanitary standards that are key for
exports. It also limits India's ability to tap the rising international demand for organic spices. Apart
from increasing output, India needs to climb the value chain in spices. Capacity must be built to
extract essential oils and oleoresins that cater to the wellness and nutraceutical industries. Most
spices have therapeutic qualities that are yet to be fully explored, never mind tapped, and that can
offer alternatives to modern medicine.


India has dominated the spice trade throughout recorded history, and these flavours have shaped
the course of history. On the surface, this domination appears intact. But cracks are appearing as
countries like China and Brazil turn their energies to a lucrative segment of farm exports. Indian
spices must remain competitive through productivity and value enhancements. The country should
also diversify its spice output away from the staple chilli, cumin, coriander, turmeric and ginger.
It should, in fact, explore growing non-native spices given its geographical diversity. That'll make
things truly spice.

LEGAL REASONING

In a historic first, the Supreme Court of India, in Harish Rana v. Union of India (2026 SCC OnLine
SC 358), permitted the withdrawal of life-sustaining medical treatment for a patient who had been
in a Persistent Vegetative State (PVS) for thirteen years following a traumatic brain injury
sustained in 2013.

continuing Clinically Assisted Nutrition and Hydration (CANH) — a form of artificial nutrition
delivered through a feeding tube — on the basis that it no longer served the patient's best interests.

prescribed and supervised by trained medical professionals. This classification was significant
because it meant CANH could be lawfully withheld or withdrawn under the passive euthanasia

(2018), which recognised the right to die with dignity as a fundamental right under Article 21 of
the Constitution. The 2026 ruling clarified that the best interests test requires decision-makers —
including doctors, medical boards, family members, and courts — to consider what the patient
himself would have wanted if he possessed decision-making capacity, a standard called

standard; the ultimate inquiry remains what course of action serves the patient's best interest.

(2026 SCC OnLine SC 466) authoritatively settled the question of whether a person born into a
Scheduled Caste community who later converts to Christianity can continue to claim Scheduled
Caste status and invoke the protections of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention
of Atrocities) Act, 1989.

The appellant, born into the Madiga community — a Scheduled Caste in Andhra Pradesh — had
converted to Christianity and served as a pastor for over a decade. Following a caste-based

certificate. The Court relied on Punjabrao v. D.P. Meshram (1964) to hold that 'professing' a
religion means making an open, public declaration of faith — the appellant's pastoral role and
decade-long service constituted such a profession.

based discrimination rooted in the Hindu social order. Since Christianity, by its theological

questions.stimulus:
Abetment of suicide is a serious criminal offence under Section 108 of the Bharatiya Nyaya
Sanhita (BNS), 2023, which replicates Section 306 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. The offence is
non-bailable, cognizable, and triable by a Court of Session. A conviction under Section 108 BNS
may attract imprisonment of up to ten years and a fine. Abetment is defined under Section 45 of
BNS to include instigating a person to commit an act, conspiring to commit an act, and
intentionally aiding the commission of an act.

The Supreme Court has consistently held that proving abetment of suicide requires establishing a
direct or proximate nexus between the accused's conduct and the victim's decision to end their life.
In Abhinav Mohan Delkar v. State of Maharashtra (2025), the Court upheld the quashing of
charges against government officials, reiterating that harassment alone — however severe —
cannot sustain a charge under Section 108 BNS unless there is a conscious, deliberate intention on
the part of the accused to drive the victim to suicide. Casual friction or professional disagreements,
without targeted and deliberate instigation, do not meet this threshold.

The Court has distinguished between two categories of relationships for the purpose of assessing
abetment: those involving sentimental or intimate ties (such as romantic or familial relationships)
and those involving official or professional relationships. A higher evidentiary standard is applied
in the latter. In official relationships, courts examine whether the accused created a situation of
unbearable and targeted harassment with the specific intent of forcing the victim to see no option
but self-destruction. The Delhi High Court in 2026 observed that a mere romantic breakup does
not, by itself, constitute instigation to suicide under Section 108 BNS.

An important related provision is Section 107 BNS, which applies when the victim is a minor, a
person of unsound mind, or a person who is intoxicated — categories considered inherently
vulnerable. Section 107 prescribes harsher punishment than Section 108, including potentially the
death penalty. The courts have cautioned against the mechanical invocation of abetment charges

by grieving families or investigative agencies without rigorous scrutiny of the legal elements,

A contract of indemnity is defined under Section 124 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, as a contract
by which one party — the indemnifier — promises to save the other party — the indemnity-holder
— from loss caused either by the promisor's own conduct or by the conduct of any other person.
This is one of the 'special contracts' recognised under Indian contract law. Section 125 supplements
this framework by specifying the rights of an indemnity-holder acting within the scope of
authority, including the right to recover damages, costs of legal proceedings, and sums paid under
compromise.

The scope of Section 124 is narrower than the English common law conception of indemnity, as
it does not explicitly cover indemnity arising from events such as fires, floods, or Acts of God —
circumstances typically governed by insurance contracts. However, courts have consistently held
that Sections 124 and 125 are not exhaustive, and equitable principles may be applied to fill gaps
in the law.

indemnification before actually suffering a loss. In the landmark case of Gajanan Moreshwar
Parelkar v. Moreshwar Madan Mantri (1942), the Bombay High Court held that when the
indemnity-holder's liability has become absolute — even if not yet discharged — the indemnifier
may be compelled to pay off the claim or place sufficient funds before the court. This principle of
'anticipatory indemnity' departs from the common law position that the indemnified party must
first discharge liability before claiming from the indemnifier.

126 of the Act. In a contract of guarantee, there are three parties — the creditor, the principal
debtor, and the surety. The surety's liability is secondary, arising only when the principal debtor
fails to perform. In a contract of indemnity, the indemnifier's liability is primary and independent.

The law of agency, governed primarily by Sections 182 to 238 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872,
establishes the legal framework for one person — the agent — to act on behalf of another — the
principal — in dealings with third parties. Section 182 defines an agent as a person employed to
do any act for another, or to represent another in dealings with third parties. The principal is bound
by the acts of the agent performed within the scope of actual or apparent authority. A contract of
agency may be created expressly, impliedly, by ratification, or by operation of law under the
doctrine of necessity.

One of the most important principles in agency law is that an agent cannot delegate their authority
to another without the express or implied consent of the principal — captured in the maxim
delegatus non potest delegare (a delegate cannot further delegate). However, Section 190 of the
Act carves out exceptions permitting sub-agency or substitution where the nature of the work
necessitates delegation, where trade usage permits it, or where the principal consents either
expressly or by conduct.

The principal is generally liable to third parties for the acts of the agent done within the scope of
apparent or ostensible authority — that is, authority which the principal has, by words or conduct,
represented the agent to possess, even if actual authority is absent. This principle, known as agency
by estoppel, protects innocent third parties who deal with the agent in good faith. However, where
the agent acts entirely outside the scope of authority and commits a fraud for entirely personal
reasons, the principal may escape liability unless the act is closely connected to duties within the
agent's employment.

Agency terminates by agreement, completion of purpose, death or insanity of either party, or by
revocation or renunciation. Section 202 of the Act creates an important exception: agency coupled
with interest — where the agent has a personal stake in the subject matter of the agency — is
irrevocable by the principal, protecting the agent's interests. Upon termination, the agent has a
right to claim remuneration for services already rendered under Section 219, and is also entitled to
a lien over the principal's property lawfully held by the agent for any amount due under Section
221.

The law of agency, governed primarily by Sections 182 to 238 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872,
establishes the legal framework for one person — the agent — to act on behalf of another — the
principal — in dealings with third parties. Section 182 defines an agent as a person employed to
do any act for another, or to represent another in dealings with third parties. The principal is bound
by the acts of the agent performed within the scope of actual or apparent authority. A contract of
agency may be created expressly, impliedly, by ratification, or by operation of law under the
doctrine of necessity.

One of the most important principles in agency law is that an agent cannot delegate their authority
to another without the express or implied consent of the principal — captured in the maxim
delegatus non potest delegare (a delegate cannot further delegate). However, Section 190 of the
Act carves out exceptions permitting sub-agency or substitution where the nature of the work
necessitates delegation, where trade usage permits it, or where the principal consents either
expressly or by conduct.

The principal is generally liable to third parties for the acts of the agent done within the scope of
apparent or ostensible authority — that is, authority which the principal has, by words or conduct,
represented the agent to possess, even if actual authority is absent. This principle, known as agency
by estoppel, protects innocent third parties who deal with the agent in good faith. However, where
the agent acts entirely outside the scope of authority and commits a fraud for entirely personal
reasons, the principal may escape liability unless the act is closely connected to duties within the
agent's employment.

Agency terminates by agreement, completion of purpose, death or insanity of either party, or by
revocation or renunciation. Section 202 of the Act creates an important exception: agency coupled
with interest — where the agent has a personal stake in the subject matter of the agency — is
irrevocable by the principal, protecting the agent's interests. Upon termination, the agent has a
right to claim remuneration for services already rendered under Section 219, and is also entitled to
a lien over the principal's property lawfully held by the agent for any amount due under Section
221.

questions.stimulus:
Vaccination is one of the most effective public health tools ever developed, yet debates about
mandatory immunisation programmes continue to generate controversy. At the heart of these
debates is the concept of herd immunity — the idea that when a sufficiently large proportion of a
population is immune to a disease, the pathogen can no longer spread freely, and even those who
cannot be vaccinated, such as newborns or immunocompromised individuals, are indirectly
protected. The threshold for herd immunity varies by disease: measles, which is highly contagious,
requires roughly 95 per cent of the population to be immune, whereas polio requires around 80 per
cent.

Proponents of mandatory vaccination argue that the decision to remain unvaccinated is not a purely
personal one. Because immunity is a collective resource, free-riding — choosing not to vaccinate
while benefiting from the protection others provide — undermines the very system that protects
the most vulnerable. They argue that just as individuals are legally required to pay taxes or stop at
red lights for the collective good, vaccination should be treated as a civic obligation when public
health is at stake.


Head Office: Plot No.6, Ground Floor, Opp. Mio Coworks, Saket, Saidulajab, New Delhi – 110030   12minutestoclat.com


Critics of mandatory vaccination, however, raise concerns about bodily autonomy and state
overreach. They argue that compelling individuals to undergo a medical procedure, however safe,
sets a troubling precedent for government intervention in personal health decisions. Some point to
vaccine hesitancy being driven not by genuine ideological objection but by misinformation and
distrust of health authorities — and that mandates may entrench resistance rather than overcome
it.

Public health researchers increasingly suggest that a better approach may lie in targeted incentives,
accessible healthcare, and transparent communication campaigns rather than legal compulsion.
Evidence from several countries shows that high vaccination rates can be achieved voluntarily
when public trust in institutions is strong and access to vaccines is equitable and convenient.
Addressing distrust and reducing access barriers may therefore prove more durable than
enforcement.

[Adapted with revisions from ‘The Ethics of Vaccine Mandates’, The Lancet, and ‘Herd Immunity
Explained’, World Health Organization.]

questions.stimulus:
Traditional economics assumes that people are rational agents who consistently make decisions in
their own best interests, carefully weighing costs and benefits before acting. Behavioural
economics challenges this assumption. Drawing on decades of research in psychology, it shows
that human decision-making is systematically influenced by cognitive shortcuts, social norms, and
the way choices are presented — none of which feature in the classical model of rational choice.

One of the most widely discussed applications of behavioural economics is ‘nudge theory’,
developed by Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein. A nudge is any change to the choice environment
— or ‘choice architecture’ — that predictably alters people’s behaviour without restricting their
freedom or changing financial incentives. Classic examples include placing healthier foods at eye
level in a cafeteria, setting pension enrolment as the default option that employees must actively
opt out of rather than opt in to, or displaying a household’s energy consumption alongside that of
its neighbours.

Nudges have achieved measurable results. In the United Kingdom, the Behavioural Insights Team
found that simply adding a line informing taxpayers that most people in their area had already paid
their taxes significantly increased on-time tax compliance. Pension auto-enrolment, introduced in
the UK in 2012, raised the proportion of eligible workers saving for retirement from under 50 per
cent to over 85 per cent within a decade.


Head Office: Plot No.6, Ground Floor, Opp. Mio Coworks, Saket, Saidulajab, New Delhi – 110030   12minutestoclat.com


Critics of nudge theory, however, argue that it is paternalistic — that nudging people towards
‘better’ choices implies that governments or institutions know best, and quietly steers individuals
without their full awareness. Others question whether nudges address root causes: a nudge might
encourage someone to enrol in a pension scheme but does nothing to raise the income from which
they save. Defenders of nudge theory respond that all choice environments contain some design,
and that making that design deliberate and evidence-based is preferable to leaving it to chance or
commercial interest.

[Adapted with revisions from Thaler & Sunstein, Nudge (2008), and ‘The Nudge Unit’, The
Economist.]

questions.stimulus:
Traditional economics assumes that people are rational agents who consistently make decisions in
their own best interests, carefully weighing costs and benefits before acting. Behavioural
economics challenges this assumption. Drawing on decades of research in psychology, it shows
that human decision-making is systematically influenced by cognitive shortcuts, social norms, and
the way choices are presented — none of which feature in the classical model of rational choice.

One of the most widely discussed applications of behavioural economics is ‘nudge theory’,
developed by Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein. A nudge is any change to the choice environment
— or ‘choice architecture’ — that predictably alters people’s behaviour without restricting their
freedom or changing financial incentives. Classic examples include placing healthier foods at eye
level in a cafeteria, setting pension enrolment as the default option that employees must actively
opt out of rather than opt in to, or displaying a household’s energy consumption alongside that of
its neighbours.

Nudges have achieved measurable results. In the United Kingdom, the Behavioural Insights Team
found that simply adding a line informing taxpayers that most people in their area had already paid
their taxes significantly increased on-time tax compliance. Pension auto-enrolment, introduced in
the UK in 2012, raised the proportion of eligible workers saving for retirement from under 50 per
cent to over 85 per cent within a decade.


Head Office: Plot No.6, Ground Floor, Opp. Mio Coworks, Saket, Saidulajab, New Delhi – 110030   12minutestoclat.com


Critics of nudge theory, however, argue that it is paternalistic — that nudging people towards
‘better’ choices implies that governments or institutions know best, and quietly steers individuals
without their full awareness. Others question whether nudges address root causes: a nudge might
encourage someone to enrol in a pension scheme but does nothing to raise the income from which
they save. Defenders of nudge theory respond that all choice environments contain some design,
and that making that design deliberate and evidence-based is preferable to leaving it to chance or
commercial interest.

[Adapted with revisions from Thaler & Sunstein, Nudge (2008), and ‘The Nudge Unit’, The
Economist.]

deployment linked incentives to offset their higher costs of tape-outs.
